opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think guaranteed-safe AI approaches can play a really important role, though I'd frame it as one important piece of a broader portfolio rather than a silver bullet.

The core idea, which a number of us tried to lay out in the "Towards Guaranteed Safe AI" paper, is that you have three components. First, a **world model**: some description of how the AI system's actions affect the world. Second, a **safety specification**: a statement of what outcomes are acceptable. Third, a **verifier**: some procedure that checks, with an auditable guarantee, that the AI's behavior satisfies the specification relative to the world model. The appeal is that instead of relying entirely on empirical testing, red-teaming, or hoping the training process instilled the right dispositions, you get a quantitative and checkable claim about safety.

Where I think this matters most is in domains where failures are catastrophic and you can't afford to learn from mistakes. Think about AI systems controlling critical infrastructure, biosecurity-relevant lab automation, or cyber-physical systems like power grids. In those settings, "it seemed fine in our evals" is not a satisfying standard. We already demand stronger assurances from aircraft software and nuclear plant controls, and I don't see why highly capable AI acting in those domains should be held to a lower bar.

That said, I want to be honest about the hard parts. The guarantees are only as good as the world model and the specification. If your world model misses some causal pathway, or your spec fails to capture what people actually care about, a formal proof gives you false confidence. So much of the interesting research is about making these components robust. That includes world models that represent their own uncertainty, which is where my background in probabilistic programming and Bayesian inference comes in. It also includes specifications that are conservative under that uncertainty: you want the system to be safe across all plausible models of the world, not just the single most likely one.

The specification problem also connects to what I care about in value alignment more broadly. Human values are pluralistic, contextual, and often contested. So I'm skeptical of approaches that try to write down a complete utility function for "the good." But I'm more optimistic about specifying *boundaries*: things like "don't cause irreversible harm to critical systems," "stay within this resource envelope," "defer to the relevant human authority here." Those are more like norms or constraints than a full objective, and people can often agree on them even when they disagree about much else.

I also think a big practical advantage of this paradigm is architectural. Rather than requiring a giant opaque model to be trustworthy end to end, you can use powerful but untrusted AI to *propose* plans, code, or designs, and then have a much smaller, more transparent component check them against the spec. That shifts the trust burden onto something we can actually inspect. You can even use AI to help build better world models and verification tools, as long as the final check is something humans can audit.

So in terms of preventing catastrophes: I see guaranteed-safe approaches as especially valuable for high-stakes, well-scoped deployments, and as a way to raise the standard of evidence we expect before deploying AI in those settings. They won't solve everything. Open-ended general assistants are much harder to bound this way, and there are governance and coordination problems no verifier can fix. But if we can carve out the most dangerous action spaces and put real guarantees around them, that meaningfully reduces the chance that capable AI ends up mediating a catastrophe.

r001.rationale: It presents guarantees as raising evidence standards and reducing catastrophe risk, but does not describe bypassing an intermediate period of avoidable AI accidents.

r002.rationale: It mentions critical infrastructure and cyber-physical systems, but says nothing about military command chains, beyond-human response speeds, or escalation into hot war.

r003.rationale: It argues these approaches can reduce catastrophe risk, but does not state that the work remains prosocial even if AI extinction risk is not considered very high.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I see guaranteed-safe approaches as playing an important but fairly specific role, and I want to be careful not to oversell them.

So the core idea behind the guaranteed-safe AI agenda, as laid out in that position paper that I co-authored with a bunch of people, is that you want to have three components. You want a world model, you want a safety specification, and you want a verifier that can produce some kind of quantitative guarantee that the AI system's behavior satisfies the specification given the world model. And the appeal of that is that you move away from relying purely on empirical evaluations, on red-teaming, on hoping that whatever you trained in generalizes the way you want. You instead get something closer to an actual proof, or at least a bounded probability of failure.

Now, where I think this is most promising is in domains where the world model is tractable and the specification is reasonably clear. So things like critical infrastructure, power grids, certain kinds of cyber-physical systems, maybe some biosecurity-adjacent contexts where you can say, this system must never output something in this class, and you can actually check that. Those are domains where the stakes are high enough and the problem is structured enough that paying the cost of formal verification makes sense. And historically, this is where formal methods have already had success, right, in things like avionics software or cryptographic protocols.

Where I'm more skeptical is the idea that you'll be able to do this for frontier general-purpose systems operating in open-ended social environments. Because there, the hard part isn't the verifier. The hard part is writing down the world model and the specification. What does it even mean to formally specify that a system doesn't manipulate people, or doesn't contribute to a slow erosion of human epistemic autonomy? Those are deeply contested normative questions, and I don't think you can offload them to a proof system. A lot of my own work has been about how you'd represent norms and intentions and values in ways that are at least somewhat structured, and even there you quickly run into the fact that human normative concepts are messy and context-dependent and often disagreed upon.

So my view is something like: guaranteed-safe approaches are a crucial piece of a defense-in-depth strategy. They can give you hard guarantees on the narrower, higher-stakes subsystems, they can constrain the action space of a more general agent, they can serve as a kind of scaffolding or containment layer. But they don't substitute for the harder governance and institutional work of deciding what we actually want these systems to do, and who gets to decide that. If anything, I worry a little about the framing where people hear the word "guaranteed" and think the problem is solved, when really what's been guaranteed is that the system satisfies a specification someone wrote down, and the question of whether that specification is the right one is still fully open.

The other thing I'd say is that I think the agenda pushes us in a healthy direction even where the full vision isn't achievable, because it forces you to be explicit. Trying to write down a world model and a spec, even if you can't fully verify against it, surfaces assumptions that would otherwise stay implicit. So I'd rather see people trying and partially failing at this than relying entirely on scale and vibes.

r001.rationale: It describes formal guarantees and defense-in-depth, but does not present them as a way to bypass an intermediate period of avoidable AI accidents.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss military command chains, fast interactions between AI systems, or escalation into hot war.

r003.rationale: It calls the agenda valuable, but does not state that prosocial reasons for the work remain even if AI extinction risk is not considered very high.

astra-6.text:
I think they could play a really important role, because they offer a way to move beyond just testing a system and hoping that we’ve covered all the ways it might fail. The aspiration is to specify what safety means, build a model of the environment in which the system operates, and then verify that its actions satisfy that specification under the assumptions of the model.

But those qualifications matter. A mathematical guarantee doesn’t automatically become a guarantee about the real world. Your model might leave something out, or your specification might fail to capture something we care about. So a central challenge is figuring out how to make those assumptions explicit and how to ensure that the system behaves conservatively when they don’t hold.

For preventing catastrophes, I think one promising role is to constrain the interface between AI systems and the world. You could have a very capable system proposing actions, but require those actions to pass through a separately verified safety mechanism before they’re executed. That way, safety doesn’t depend entirely on understanding the internal reasoning of the system proposing them.

I’d see this as one layer of protection, alongside evaluations, monitoring, and governance. It’s particularly valuable where we can define concrete constraints. It’s much harder to provide a comprehensive guarantee against all the ways AI could contribute to a catastrophe, especially through people and institutions. But that shouldn’t stop us from building strong guarantees for the parts we can characterize.

r001.rationale: The response describes verification as a complement to testing and other safeguards, but does not present it as bypassing an intermediate period of avoidable AI accidents.

r002.rationale: It does not mention military command chains, AI interactions at beyond-human speeds, or escalation into hot war.

r003.rationale: It does not state that the work has a prosocial justification even if AI extinction risk is not believed to be very high.

sol-6.1.text:
I think guaranteed-safe AI approaches are a really important part of the picture. The basic idea is that, rather than just training a system to behave safely and then testing it, we want some explicit specification of what safety means, a model of how the system interacts with the world, and a way to verify that its actions satisfy that specification.

That could be particularly valuable when an AI is acting through tools or controlling physical infrastructure. You might have a very capable system proposing actions, but those actions have to pass through a verification process before they can be executed. So safety doesn’t depend entirely on whether the model has learned the right intentions.

The crucial caveat is that a guarantee is only as good as its assumptions. Did we specify the right thing? Does our model capture the relevant features of the world? A mathematical proof can be correct while the system is still unsafe because something important was left out.

So I see these approaches as a way to build stronger layers of protection, rather than a complete solution by themselves. We still need alignment, oversight, and institutions that decide which risks are acceptable. But wherever we can turn a hoped-for safety property into a checkable constraint, that seems like a very valuable step toward preventing catastrophes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses verification as a layer of protection but does not say it would bypass an intermediate period of avoidable AI accidents.

r002.rationale: It mentions tools and physical infrastructure, but not military command chains, interactions at speeds beyond human response, or escalation into hot war.

r003.rationale: It calls guaranteed-safe approaches valuable but does not connect their justification to prosocial benefits independent of belief in high AI extinction risk.
